text.p: Vencor Inc's deep pockets and experience operating long-term care hospitals give it the edge over Select Medical Corp in their battle to take over Transitional Hospitals Corp, analysts and arbitrageurs said.

While privately-held Select may try to top Vencor's $16 per share hostile cash tender, which is above Select's $14.55-per-share merger agreement, Vencor's financial firepower likely will prevail with a winning bid, they said.
Transitional, based in Las Vegas, did not return telephone messages seeking comment and Select, based in Mechanicsburg, Pa., could not immediately comment.
"Vencor has the better offer and the higher price," said Raymond James analyst John Ransom. "They clearly have the ability to pay more than anybody."
Vencor said early Wednesday that is has begun a cash tender offer to acquire all outstanding shares of Transitional for $639 million.

Earlier this week Transitional said it signed a cash merger agreement with Select at $14.55 per share, an announcement that included Transitional's comment that it received a $15 per share offer from another party after the Select merger agreement was signed.

Ransom said Vencor at $16 per share would pay a little over two times annual revenues, a price that would be about $0.05 to $0.07 dilutive to Vencor's 1997 per-share earnings and $0.03 to $0.04 dilutive in 1998.
According Zack's Investment Research, analysts expect Vencor to earn a consensus $2.20 in 1997 and $2.62 in 1998.

Vencor's stock "is acting like it's a done deal," Ransom said, referring to a sharp selloff driven by the anticipated earnings dilution. In afternoon trade, Vencor shares were off three, or seven percent, to 40 while Transitional gained 1-1/4, or 8.7 percent, to 15-5/8.
Transitional's earlier intraday high of 15-3/4 was a new year-high, topping the old 12-month peak of 14-5/8.
"I absolutely agree with it (the Vencor/Transitional deal). The margins are north of 20 percent and it (the long-term hospital business) feeds their other business," Ransom added.

John Hindelong of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, said, "Vencor appears to be very committed. They put a higher cash offer on the table and it makes sense from Vencor's point of view because it is the pioneer in long-term care hospitals."
The transaction would probably dilute Vencor's 1997 earnings per share by $0.05 to $0.10 and by "a few cents" in 1998, Hindelong said.
"I dont think Select has the ammo to go higher than $16 and I don't think you get a raised bid. It is a $16 deal," said an arbitrageur who declined to be identified.
Select has the financial backing of, among others, New York-based Welsh Carson Anderson & Stowe, a firm Ransom described as "the leading healthcare venture capitalist firm."
No one was immediately available to comment at Welsh Carson.
As for Select's chairman Rocco Ortenzio, he is a seasoned health-care executive who recently was with Continental Medical Systems Inc, acquired by Horizon/CMS Healthcare Corp in 1995.

"Rocco Ortenzio has been in this business for a long time. He is an old name in the industry, very aggressive and very acquisitive. He has been through several mergers and knows how to do a deal," said a second arb who requested anonymity.
